source.title: Backward Oversmoothing: why is it hard to train deep Graph Neural Networks?

record.file_problem: Full text is present. The supplied text identifies the paper as v2, dated 13 Mar 2026.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own deep GNN training results and argues that vanilla deep GNNs can quickly reach near-stationary points with high loss. Its experiments use regression on graph datasets, so they do not directly test the listed CIFAR classification versions; they refine the broader claim by identifying a graph-network setting where training can stall.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports forward and backward oversmoothing metrics and theoretical stationary-point results; numerical values visible only in plots are recorded as figure-only. Dataset properties in Table 1 are not training-outcome rows. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes optimization in deep graph neural networks, but none of V1–V6 is tested. Its regression losses and stationary-point results do not measure CIFAR classification error, teacher-student width effects, convolutional depth degradation, initialization comparisons, learning-rate thresholds, or batch-normalization benefits. Related GNN results cannot establish or challenge those versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. Under stated assumptions, the authors prove that output-layer stationarity implies near-stationarity throughout deep vanilla GNNs, construct high-loss near-stationary regions, and attribute this mechanism to backward oversmoothing. They provide an MLP counterexample and numerical illustrations, leaving detailed mitigation analysis for future work. Near-stationarity alone does not prove a spurious local minimum.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies vanilla graph neural networks on graph datasets, with full-gradient MSE regression and weights initialized as Id + εN. It does not use the listed classification benchmarks or training recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that the high-loss stationary-point effect is more pronounced when λ is smaller (notably on the synthetic datasets and WikiCS) and less clear on Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed, where λ is close to 1. In the skip-connection illustration, behavior depends on weight amplitude s; an unbalanced or too-large s can cause signal explosion.

fits_no_version.finding: Deep vanilla GNNs quickly approach high-loss near-stationary points relative to MLP counterparts, most clearly on WikiCS and the synthetic graphs; the effect is less clear on Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under the reported full-gradient regression setup and near-identity initialization, deep vanilla GNNs can stall at high training loss, with stronger effects on graphs having smaller smoothing rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Under explicit smoothing and weight-norm assumptions, stationarity of the output layer implies near-stationarity throughout sufficiently deep GNNs. A centered-regression construction has high-loss near-stationary regions; an MLP counterexample lacks the same implication.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Backward oversmoothing creates high-loss near-stationary regions specific to the analyzed class of deep GNNs.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix B reports that skip connections counter forward and backward oversmoothing and appear to avoid vanilla-GNN stationary points at initialization scale s = 5/L, while loss still plateaus relative to MLPs. Larger scales can cause signal explosion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Skip connections can improve deep GNN optimization in a scale-dependent manner without fully eliminating training plateaus.

record.problems: The experimental illustrations convert classification dataset labels to regression targets and report training loss rather than classification error. Numerical training-loss values are presented only in plots. The authors say the effect is less clear on Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed. The experiments use full gradients and label every node; the text notes that the results concern vanilla GNNs and do not analyze mitigation strategies.
record.rows_left_out: No result rows were left out. Figure 1's WikiCS example is not duplicated because the Appendix B experiments include WikiCS in R1.

untested.parts: Training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/100, including random labels and the stated size and training-recipe qualifications.
Spurious-local-minimum frequencies in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and effects of one or two extra student neurons.
Training-error comparisons across depths in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks and matched identity-shortcut networks; the tanh and Fixup qualifications.
Activation-matched initialization comparisons, their effects on learning speed and trainable depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
Initial stability thresholds, catapult recovery, curvature trajectories, edge-of-stability training, and divergence below or above thresholds.
Matched batch-normalization comparisons of training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup training without normalization.

record.verdict_notes: The skip-connection illustrations concern GNN regression and do not test V3's convolutional training-error comparisons. Near-identity initialization is held fixed rather than compared against alternatives, so it does not test V4. No omitted result bears directly on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/100 classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size, optimizer comparisons, and effects of early stopping or regularization.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious-minimum rates, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual convolutional networks on ImageNet or CIFAR-10, and the stated shortcut comparisons.
Comparisons of initialization methods, signal and gradient propagation, and trainable depth in plain networks.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, catapult dynamics, sharpness, and divergence conditions.
Batch-normalization comparisons, accuracy speed, learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup residual networks.

rows.subject: GNN
rows.operation_detail: Trained with full gradients on the WikiCS graph dataset; labels were converted to integers and treated as a regression problem.

conditions.value: weights initialized as Id + εN, with ε small and s ≈ 1

rows.baseline: MLP counterpart, shown in the same figure; numerical reference not stated
rows.uncertainty: Averaged over 10 random initializations for the plotted illustration; no error bars stated
rows.locator: Appendix B, Fig. 2 (bottom row, right panel); text discussion in Appendix B, “GNN training, comparison with MLP”
rows.note: The authors say the GNN tends to quickly reach a stationary point with high loss compared with its MLP counterpart; they say the effect is greatly accentuated on WikiCS. No numerical loss values are stated in the text.
rows.check: WikiCS GNN regression loss bears on no listed version; partial is therefore inappropriate. Figure 2 specifies averaging over 10 initializations for the oversmoothing panels, without clearly extending that statement to training losses.
